tldr: A sampling-based MPC method that projects velocities into the equality tangent subspace and inequality half-spaces inside MPPI rollouts, then retracts finite-step drift back onto the manifold, strictly satisfying geometric equality and inequality constraints to numerical tolerance even under strong task costs.
hero_caption: Overview of PR-MPPI and the Active Constraint Projector pipeline. Inside rollouts and on the executed command, sampled velocities are first projected onto the equality tangent subspace and corrected into active CBF inequality half-spaces without breaking the subspace, before a final retraction pulls states back onto the manifold to numerical tolerance.
overview:
Controlling dual-arm robots to carry objects requires satisfying closed-chain equality constraints (strictly maintaining relative end-effector poses) while simultaneously respecting inequality constraints like joint limits and collision avoidance. This is one of the most critical challenges in robotics. Sampling-based Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is widely used thanks to GPU parallelization and its ability to handle non-convex costs. However, standard MPPI treats constraints as soft penalties in the cost function, which fundamentally fail when a strong task-tracking cost overpowers the penalties.

To solve this, this paper proposes Projection-Retraction MPPI (PR-MPPI). The core idea is to enforce constraints directly inside the rollout dynamics rather than delegating them to the cost function. Specifically, sampled joint velocities are first projected onto the tangent subspace of the equality constraint, and then projected into the active inequality half-spaces within that subspace. This structurally prevents inequality corrections (such as joint-limit avoidance) from violating the closed-chain equality. Furthermore, because first-order velocity projections leave a small drift off the equality constraint under finite-time integration, a Gauss–Newton retraction is applied to the returned command, restoring the equality constraint strictly to machine numerical tolerance.

In simulation, across joint-limit stress tests and 30 randomized obstacle avoidance runs on a 14-DoF dual-arm Franka setup, PR-MPPI never crossed inequality boundaries under aggressive tracking goals and kept equality command residuals down to the $10^{-11}$ level. On real hardware, arms of a Unitree H1-2 humanoid reactively avoided a moving obstacle at 30 Hz while holding a tray with both hands.
contributions: Built a constraint-aware rollout mechanism that projects sampled velocities into the equality tangent subspace and nested active CBF half-spaces, ensuring inequality handling never breaks equalities.

Eliminated finite-step integration drift off the equality manifold using Gauss–Newton retraction, strictly satisfying equality constraints to numerical tolerance at the command level independent of MPPI task weighting.
Theoretically proved that inequality constraint error induced by finite-step integration and retraction is bounded by $O(\Delta t^2)$, showing it can be completely absorbed by a small safety buffer.

Demonstrated stable real-time operation (30 Hz) for equality preservation, joint-limit protection, and dynamic obstacle avoidance on both a 14-DoF dual-arm simulation and a real Unitree H1-2 humanoid.

sections.heading: Beyond Soft Penalties: Why Does MPPI Need Exact Manifold Control?
sections.summary: While MPPI excels at handling complex contacts and non-convex costs, it treats constraints only as cost penalties that fail under strong task demands. Prior barrier function and projection methods either focused only on inequalities or left equality drift unresolved. This paper tackles the challenge by combining in-rollout dual projection with execution-level retraction.
sections.details:
Manipulation tasks often impose constraints that must hold strictly throughout the motion. For instance, when transporting a rigid object clamped between two arms, the closed kinematic chain maintaining the relative pose of both end-effectors must hold exactly; otherwise, internal forces build up and the grasp fails. At the same time, inequality constraints like joint limits and obstacle clearances must never be crossed.

Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control samples many control inputs and computes a cost-weighted average. It is widely popular in modern robotics because it is gradient-free and runs fast on GPUs. However, standard MPPI penalizes constraint violations through soft penalties in the cost function. Under a strong task cost driving the robot toward a goal, constraint penalties are easily overpowered, leading to violations.

To enforce inequalities more strictly, prior works introduced CBF (Control Barrier Function) filters or projected samples back into safe sets. However, these only provide one-sided inequality margins and lack mechanisms to preserve geometric equality constraints.

In classical redundant manipulator control, Jacobian null-space projections are common, and geometric motion planning uses manifold projections and retractions. Yet incorporating them into sampling-based MPC remains very limited. Prior works such as DQ-MPPI and MC-MPPI suffered from incomplete inequality handling or could not fully eliminate finite-step drift off equalities.

This paper proposes PR-MPPI, which performs dual projections onto the equality tangent space and inequality half-spaces inside rollout dynamics, followed by a Gauss–Newton retraction onto the manifold.

captions.F1: PR-MPPI control loop overview. Sampled joint velocities pass through the active constraint projector $\Pi_{\mathrm{act}}$ at each rollout step. After averaging, the command is projected again along the real state, and the final command is retracted onto the manifold.

sections.heading: Fusing Projection and Retraction: An Algorithm That Protects Inequalities Without Breaking Equalities
sections.summary: Inside discrete-time dynamics, sampled velocities are projected onto the intersection of the equality null space and active CBF inequality half-spaces. The MPPI-weighted nominal command is re-projected at the execution layer and retracted onto the manifold via Gauss–Newton iterations. Finite-step error is theoretically proven to stay within $O(\Delta t^2)$.
sections.details:
The PR-MPPI framework consists of two main stages: constraint-aware rollout dynamics and execution-layer projection/retraction.

### II-A Problem Formulation
With joint angles $\bm{q}_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ as states and joint velocities $\bm{u}_t = \dot{\bm{q}}_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ as control inputs, the goal over a prediction horizon $T$ is to minimize expected trajectory cost while strictly satisfying equality constraints $\bm{c}(\bm{q}_t) = \bm{0}$ and inequality constraints $\bm{h}(\bm{q}_t) \geq \bm{0}$.

### II-B Constraint-Aware Rollout Projection
Rather than penalizing infeasible samples via cost, PR-MPPI forces samples into the feasible set from the start.
- **Stage 1 (Equality Tangent Space Projection)**: Using the null-space projection matrix $\bm{N} = \bm{I} - \bm{J}_c^\dagger \bm{J}_c$ of the equality constraint Jacobian $\bm{J}_c$, the sampled velocity $\tilde{\bm{u}}_t$ is first projected onto the tangent space vector $\tilde{\bm{u}}_{p,t} = \bm{N}\tilde{\bm{u}}_t$. This yields $\bm{J}_c \tilde{\bm{u}}_{p,t} = \bm{0}$, preserving the equality to first order.
- **Stage 2 (Active Inequality Correction)**: Inequalities are formulated as discrete-time CBF half-spaces $\nabla \bar{h}_i^T \bm{u} \geq -\gamma_i \bar{h}_i$. Solving for all inequalities every time is computationally heavy, so an active set $\mathcal{A}$ of high-residual constraints is formed to compute KKT-satisfying corrections within the tangent space. Because every correction term is pre-multiplied by $\bm{N}$, inequality corrections never violate the equality tangent condition $\bm{J}_c \tilde{\bm{u}}^+_t = \bm{0}$.

Exponential cost weighting is then applied across these corrected rollouts to obtain the nominal input sequence $\bm{U}^*$.

### II-C Execution-Layer Projection and Retraction
The MPPI-averaged input is merely a mean across states visited by individual samples, so it does not satisfy constraints by itself. Thus, an execution-layer projection is applied again along the predicted trajectory starting from the current state $\bm{q}_0$.

However, even if the velocity satisfies $\bm{J}_c \bm{u}^*_0 = \bm{0}$, integrating over a finite time step $\Delta t$ induces an $O(\Delta t^2)$ drift off the equality manifold. PR-MPPI therefore applies a Gauss–Newton retraction $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (Eq. 15) to the next target position until the equality residual drops below a numerical tolerance $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}$ (machine precision level).

**Lemma 1 (Bounded Inequality Error)**: Joint displacement caused by retraction is bounded by $O(\Delta t^2)$. Therefore, the inequality violation at the next step is bounded by $-\kappa_i \Delta t^2$, which is proven to be completely absorbed by a pre-set safety margin $h_{\mathrm{safe}}$.

sections.heading: From Stress Tests to Real Humanoids: Validating Constraint Satisfaction and Real-Time Performance
sections.summary: Three experiments were conducted on a simulated 14-DoF dual-arm Franka and a real Unitree H1-2 humanoid. In joint-limit stress tests, PR-MPPI maintained equalities to machine precision (order of $10^{-11}$) and achieved a 100% success rate across 30 randomized obstacle runs. On the real humanoid, it reactively avoided dynamic obstacles at 30 Hz.
sections.details:
All experiments evaluate a task where dual arms rigidly grasp a tray horizontally (closed-chain equality constraint in Eq. 17). The controller runs at 30 Hz ($\Delta t = 1/30$ s) with $K = 1000$ rollouts and horizon $T = 30$.

### III-B Experiment 1: Joint-Limit Stress Test
The task aggressively pulls the tray downward toward a target ($-2.41$ rad) that exceeds the joint 4 limit (lower bound $-2.35$ rad, CBF safety boundary $-2.30$ rad) on both arms.
- **Results**: DQ-MPPI and an ablation without inequality projection violated the limit by $0.082$ rad and $0.022$ rad, respectively, overpowered by tracking demand. Full PR-MPPI smoothly stopped at the $-2.30$ rad safety boundary, with a boundary violation of only $0.003$ rad (well within the $0.05$ rad safety margin).
- **Command Equality Residual**: With retraction, Full PR-MPPI achieved translational residuals of $(0.170 \pm 0.070) \times 10^{-10}$ m and rotational residuals of $(0.280 \pm 0.020) \times 10^{-10}$ rad, reaching the machine numerical precision floor (zero). In contrast, methods without retraction and DQ-MPPI left residuals on the order of $10^{-3}$.
- **Computation Speed**: DQ-MPPI required 238.9 ms per update (approx. 4.2 Hz), whereas PR-MPPI completed in 19.35 ms, easily maintaining the 30 Hz rate.

### III-C Experiment 2: Randomized Obstacle Avoidance (30 Trials)
A spherical obstacle blocked the tray's straight path. MC-MPPI got stuck when the obstacle was centered because samples could not pass, succeeding in only 13/30 trials. DQ-MPPI often dropped the tray due to broken equality constraints during sharp motions, succeeding in 18/30 trials. Full PR-MPPI, which projects samples within rollouts, only evaluated feasible trajectories and achieved a 100% success rate (30/30 trials) by smoothly detouring around obstacles.

### III-D Experiment 3: Dynamic Avoidance on Real Humanoid (Unitree H1-2)
When a human moved an obstacle toward the tray, PR-MPPI reconfigured dual-arm postures in real time (30 Hz) to avoid collisions while keeping the closed-chain constraint and tray horizontal.
However, when an obstacle approached from an angle where the grasp equality geometrically forbade backward motion, the tangent gradient $\bm{N}\nabla \bar{h}$ vanished, revealing a structural limitation where avoidance became impossible.

sections.heading: Takeaways and Future Outlook: Expanding from Kinematics to Torque Control
sections.summary: PR-MPPI demonstrates that integrating dual velocity projection and retraction enables sampling-based MPC to satisfy equality constraints to numerical tolerance while strictly holding inequality margins. Future work points toward extending from kinematics to torque and contact-force levels, as well as relaxing equalities when avoidance is geometrically trapped.
sections.details:
This paper presented PR-MPPI, a sampling-based MPC combining nested velocity-space projections inside rollout dynamics with Gauss–Newton retraction on final commands. Experiments on a 14-DoF dual-arm system showed that closed-chain equality constraints are maintained to machine precision under strong task costs, while inequality constraints like joint limits and collision avoidance remain strictly enforced.

Real-robot experiments on the Unitree H1-2 also highlighted a structural trade-off: strictly enforcing equality constraints prevents avoidance motions when an obstacle approaches along directions that leave no feasible tangent degrees of freedom.

The current implementation operates at the kinematic level with velocity commands. However, the projection-retraction framework naturally extends to torque control using dynamically consistent tangent spaces. Future directions include directly enforcing torque limits and contact force boundaries as inequalities at the torque level, as well as introducing mechanisms to selectively relax grasp constraints when escape motions are blocked.

takeaways: When soft penalty-based constraints fail in sampling-based MPC, embedding constraint projections directly into rollout dynamics is highly effective.
When handling both equalities and inequalities, pre-multiplying inequality corrections with the equality null-space matrix prevents inequality handling from destroying equality constraints.
Rather than stopping at first-order velocity projections, adding a single Gauss–Newton retraction step eliminates finite-step drift and guarantees machine-precision equality satisfaction.
Generating only inequality-compliant samples inside rollouts confines exploration to the feasible region, drastically reducing freeze/stuck behavior in tight spaces or near obstacles.
limitations: Prioritizing strict equality satisfaction makes avoidance impossible if no escape direction exists within the equality-admissible tangent subspace.
The current implementation is at the kinematic (velocity) level, meaning low-level torque tracking errors act as disturbances and prevent real-world constraint residuals from being strictly zero.
Solving active-set projections for inequalities at every rollout step increases computational overhead as the number of inequality constraints grows, even with GPU parallelization.
